storm.summary_layperson: No storms are on radar right now, and while there's a slight chance of an isolated shower or rumble of thunder later this evening, nothing organized is tracking toward the cove.
storm.local_effect_blurb: The Sound's marine layer is already thin — only a 3.6°F air–water gap at 4 PM, and the projection shows air temp dropping below the water temp by evening — so there's no meaningful buffer left for anything that develops later tonight.
storm.detail_html:
KOKX radar is clean as of the latest scan — no storm cells being tracked toward the cove. The NWS Area Forecast Discussion carries a slight chance of an isolated shower or thunderstorm through this evening and again Tuesday afternoon, with a more organized frontal system not expected until Thursday.

Instability is low (CAPE 600 J/kg) even though shear is elevated for that amount of fuel (32 kt through 0–6 km) — the AFD itself describes the setup as a "marginally unstable/modest shear" environment, good for at most an isolated strong gust rather than anything widespread.

The Sound's usual defense — a cool marine layer that chokes incoming storms — isn't much of a factor tonight. The air–water gap is only 3.6°F right now (water 75.2°F, air 78.8°F), which is already below the 5°F threshold this framework treats as a meaningful buffer, and the trend projects the gap going negative by 8 PM as the air cools faster than the Sound holds its heat. There's essentially no protective mechanism standing by tonight, active or not.

Net call for the window: low risk regionally and locally, most likely a quiet, dry evening with at most an isolated sprinkle or distant rumble. The cove isn't getting any special edge over surrounding towns tonight since there's no cell in play to benefit from Sound cooling in the first place, and the buffer is too weak to matter even if one did develop.

What would change this call: any new cell appearing on KOKX radar approaching from the W–NW–SW, or CAPE building well past the 1,500 J/kg punch-through range tonight or into Tuesday's slight chance.

wind.tactics_blurb: RYC now: S 188° at 11.5 kt (avg 9.9, gusting 14) — moderate gradient wind, no sea breeze in play (deltaT only 3.6°F, below the 5°F gate). Backs SW through the evening and eases fast, into drifter range (4 kt or less) by 7 PM and staying light the rest of the window. Favor the middle of the course as flow backs toward W — get racing done early, the back half risks postponement-level light air.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
The air–water temperature difference (deltaT) is only 3.6°F right now, below the 5°F gate this framework requires for a thermal circulation to be in play. Despite a borderline 57% of coastal stations reading southerly, that's not enough on its own — deltaT is the gate, and it isn't met. So today classifies as a gradient-only day, not a sea-breeze day. The authoritative airport-network gradient (9.4 kt) puts it in the moderate bucket: raceable, but no thermal engine behind it.

RYC right now reads S 188° at 11.5 kt (10-min avg 9.9, gusting 14), noticeably backed from the western-LIS ensemble median of SW 229° — that zone's direction agreement is only 0.60, below the threshold where this framework flags a coherent wind field. That's a sign of some local eddying or a soft boundary near the cove rather than clean regional flow. Trust RYC for what the fleet actually feels at the line right now.

HRRR shows this gradient flow easing and backing through the evening: SW around 8 kt at 5 PM, sliding to WSW/W and down to roughly 4 kt by 7–8 PM. This is a genuine gradient relaxation, not a thermal sunset collapse — there's no sea breeze here to die, the wind is just running out of synoptic push. Model data cuts off at 8 PM (f06–f12 failed to fetch this run); the 9–10 PM figures continue the same backing/easing trend by extrapolation, so treat the back half of the table as a softer call than the first half.

Late August sits inside the seasonal window for a backdoor cold front, but the hot-inland ingredient isn't met (temp differential 3.6°F, below the 5°F trigger gate) — no live backdoor signal tonight.

In racing terms: 6–8 kt through 6 PM is still solid one-design sailing, but conditions slide into drifter territory (4 kt or under) by 7 PM and stay there, with direction wandering WSW–W–WNW as the light flow settles for the night. Favor the middle of the course as the wind backs toward W — that direction typically develops holes near the CT shore per the cove's geography, so mid-Sound pressure away from the shore will be more reliable. Get racing done in the first couple hours; the back half of the window risks AP-level light air.

data_caveats: HRRR forecast wind/temperature data available only through 8:00 PM local (f01–f05); f06–f12 fetch/parse failed, so the 9:00 and 10:00 PM wind figures are extrapolated from the trend, not raw model output.
HRRR's hour-one wind speed (8.9 kt) runs below the live RYC reading (11.5 kt, gusting 14) — treat the hourly table as a lower-bound trend, not an exact match to what the fleet will feel at the start.
